title: ECI’s software use needs reconsideration
shows: Joseph C. Mathew, a former IT adviser to the Government of Keralam, argues that the Commission's use of software needs to be reconsidered. He writes that under section 13B of the Representation of the People Act the sole authority for editing the voters' list is entrusted to local Electoral Registration Officers and Booth Level Officers, and that the Commission's centralised ECINet and ERONet software has effectively stripped them of their legally mandated powers. In his view the Commission appears in the process to have created its own Act and Rules. He recalls that in 2015 the Commission linked voter IDs with Aadhaar data under the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme, which he describes as a mass elimination of voters using centralised software, until the Supreme Court put an end to it. Most of the piece concerns electronic voting machines, where he argues from two Supreme Court judgments that the safeguards the Commission has presented do not make the system foolproof. He closes by saying that a reconsideration is necessary at a time when the Commission is using software “to dictate addition in the electoral list itself”.
quote: Under 13B of the Representation of the People Act, the sole authority for editing the voters’ list is entrusted to local Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Booth Level Officers (BLOs). However, the ECI’s centralised ECINet and ERONet software architectures have effectively stripped them of their legally mandated powers.

The ECI had resorted to mass elimination of voters using a centralised software in 2015 itself by linking voter IDs with Aadhaar data under the National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentic Program, before the top court put an end to it.
Therefore, a reconsideration is necessary, particularly at a time when the ECI is using software to dictate addition in the electoral list itself.
note: First reading, 23 November 2026, rewritten at the second reading on the session lead's decision. Subscription. The two judgments in the part on the machines are Kamal Nath vs Election Commission of India and ADR vs. Election Commission, and his argument there about the symbol loading unit and the bitmap file is not carried. Every claim is his, and the summary carries no verdict on it.

title: Voters and Citizens: From Inclusion to Exclusion in Contemporary India
shows: Niraja Gopal Jayal, who holds the Avantha Chair at King's College London, argues in an essay first published in Indian Politics and Policy in spring 2026, and republished with a postscript written in November 2026, that the revision of the rolls shares the exclusionary tendencies that she traces in India's citizenship law since 1985. She sets the inclusive making of the first roll from 1947 against the Assam National Register of Citizens and the amendments of 1985, 2003 and 2019, and reads the Supreme Court's judgment of 27 May 2026 as endorsing the Commission's power to examine citizenship before it enrols a voter. In her account the revision moved the work of verification from the booth level officer's visits to the voter, who is deleted for failing to submit the enumeration form, and the Commission's change to Form 7 in 2022 let anyone from the same assembly constituency object to a name. She gives West Bengal's figures as about 6.4 million routine deletions, 2.7 million names under adjudication and 0.188 million added, and counts 7.4 million deleted in Tamil Nadu and 6.81 million in Gujarat. She writes that the burden falls disproportionately on Dalits, Muslims and women, and that the abuse of Form 7 by Booth Level Agents of the BJP to target Muslim voters has been reported from several states. In the postscript she puts Karnataka's deletions at one crore, about 18% of the electorate, says the roll is being used to deny welfare benefits although the Supreme Court ruled the revision cannot be used for other purposes, and says that only scrapping the revision and returning to the earlier rolls can put this right.
quote: This paper draws attention to a disconcerting parallel between the historical evolution of Indian citizenship and that of the process by which the electoral rolls are revised and the Indian voter is identified.
In 2022, the Election Commission amended its Form 7 to state that such objections could be filed by anyone from the same assembly constituency.

title: For N Chandrababu Naidu’s 2024 Win, the ECI Recorded an Impossibility After 6 PM. Then Did Not Investigate
shows: It concerns polling-day records of the 2024 elections and does not cover the roll revisions. In Part 3 of its Election Audit series, the Reporters' Collective reports that two returning officers' reports sent to the Commission a day apart give different counts of voters still in the queue at 6 pm in Chittoor in Andhra Pradesh, where the Lok Sabha and Assembly polls were held together at the same booths. It says the report for the Chittoor Lok Sabha seat counted 56,067 such voters and the report for the seven Assembly seats that make up Chittoor counted 24,596, a gap of more than 31,000, and that the Commission never looked into it. It explains that the presiding officer hands numbered slips to the voters in the queue at the close of poll and records the number issued in the diary, which the returning officer scrutinises the next day. It notes that N. Chandrababu Naidu of the Telugu Desam Party won Kuppam, one of the seven Assembly seats, and became Chief Minister, and that the party won the Lok Sabha seat and all seven Assembly seats. The Collective says it has so far reviewed the returning officers' reports for only one parliamentary seat, that the Commission did not answer its questions, and that the Chief Electoral Officer's office referred it to the district election officer.
quote: In the report for the Chittoor Lok Sabha seat, officials said 56,067 voters were still in the queue at 6 pm, waiting to vote after dark. In the other report, for the seven assembly seats that make up Chittoor, they told the ECI only 24,596 voters stayed on to vote late into the night.
We have so far reviewed reports of returning officers for only one parliamentary seat. What transpired in other constituencies is not yet clear.
note: First reading, 23 November 2026. Read in full from the Collective's page with curl on 23 November 2026, reached from the homepage. The page is marked Part 3, Election Audit, and prints November 23, 2026, byline Sumedha Mittal and Venkatesh Nayak, edited by Furquan Ameen. The article is about the 2024 polls and holds no figure on the electoral rolls, so nothing in it can be checked against the site's data, and every figure is the Collective's. Not carried are the Andhra Pradesh Chief Electoral Officer's statement, as the article reports it, that machine faults and violence kept polling going late, in one case until 2 am, and the opposition's claim of rigging.
